account: Zhang et al. 2025 supply the corpus's boundary-condition evidence: a systematic evaluation across 4 models, 9 benchmarks, and 5 MAD methods finds MAD generally fails to beat simple single-agent baselines CoT and SC, with the failures varying by task type (worse on programming, better on math) and unaffected by hyperparameter tuning. The authors identify model heterogeneity (Heter-MAD) as a consistently effective remedy, improving all tested MAD frameworks, with gains attributed to correcting CW/WC questions. Findings are anchored to PDF pages 1, 3, 7, 9, 11, and 12.

citations.excerpt: Surprisingly, our findings reveal that MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency, even when consuming significantly more inference-time computation.

claims.statement: Zhang et al. report that 'current MAD research suffers from critical limitations in evaluation practices' and that 'MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Consistency, even when consuming significantly more inference-time computation.'

citations.excerpt: As summarized in Figure 1, none of these MAD methods achieve a win rate higher than 20% when compared to CoT across 36 scenarios (4 models × 9 benchmarks). Further experiments varying the number of agents and debate rounds show that simply adjusting these hyperparameters can hardly reverse this negative outcome.

claims.statement: Across 36 configurations (4 models × 9 benchmarks), none of the MAD methods achieve a win rate higher than 20% against CoT, and the negative result persists when varying agents and debate rounds.

citations.excerpt: When examining performance by task type, MAD frameworks performed worse on programming tasks (only SoM/AgentVerse had positive win rates) but better on mathematical reasoning, surpassing their overall performance levels.

claims.statement: Task type is a boundary condition: MAD performed worse on programming tasks, with only SoM/AgentVerse having positive win rates, but better on mathematical reasoning.

citations.excerpt: The sole notable exception is observed with EoT on the GSM8K benchmark, where increasing the number of agents from 3 to 9 leads to a continuous improvement in performance, ultimately surpassing CoT. ... increasing the number of agents or debate rounds often results in either stagnation or even a decline in performance.

claims.statement: Increasing agents or debate rounds generally yields stagnation or decline, except EoT on GSM8K, ruling out hyperparameter tuning as a universal explanation for MAD's inferiority to CoT.

citations.excerpt: We observe that SC effectively utilizes the increased inference budget. However, MAD frameworks either: (i) show no positive trend in achieving stable performance improvements ... or (ii) continue to underperform SC while consuming a comparable number of tokens ... These observations indicate that, in comparison to SC, MAD is generally a less efficient method for leveraging token consumption.

claims.statement: Beyond performance, MAD is generally a less efficient method for leveraging token consumption than Self-Consistency, which positively scales with budget while MAD often shows no stable gains.

citations.excerpt: Notably, we find that Heter-MAD consistently improves the performance of all considered MAD frameworks. Specifically, ... Heter-SoM improves SoM-average ... by 6.4%, and Heter-EoT improves EoT-average by 8.2%.
The primary booster of Heter-MAD's performance gains is its ability to effectively handle CW and WC questions, which together account for a significant portion of the dataset.

claims.statement: Model heterogeneity (Heter-MAD) consistently improves all tested MAD frameworks; for example Heter-SoM improves SoM-average by 6.4% and Heter-EoT by 8.2%, and gains are attributed to handling questions only one model solves (CW/WC).

citations.excerpt: We hypothesize that the significant performance gain of Heter-SoM and Heter-EoT stems from the rather simple design of SoM and EoT, and thus they are more compatible with heterogeneous models. Conversely, more complex frameworks ... struggle with compatibility.

claims.statement: Complex MAD frameworks (ChatEval, AgentVerse) benefit less from heterogeneity than simple ones (SoM, EoT), likely due to compatibility issues in aggregating heterogeneous models.

citations.excerpt: we observe that, in general, these MAD frameworks are able to outperform single-agent (SA) that are instructed to directly generate their answers. Specifically, we observe that MAD frameworks outperform SA in most conditions (34 out of 45 conditions utilizing GPT-4o-mini), which perfectly aligns with previous findings in the field.

claims.statement: Zhang et al. also find that MAD can outperform direct single-agent prompting (SA) in most conditions, replicating prior positive findings, which qualifies the negative result.

counterevidence: Positive MAD results (Du et al. 2023) exist in the corpus; Zhang et al.'s null is limited to the evaluated conditions and may not generalize to all setups.
The heterogeneity gains in Zhang et al. are for GPT-4o-mini + Llama3.1-70b pair; gains for other model pairs are untested in the dossier.
unresolved: Whether Zhang et al.'s null results are specific to the 9 benchmarks or extend to more complex reasoning tasks (they themselves note benchmarks may be too simple).
The exact compute parity conditions (LLM calls vs tokens) across MAD and baselines are not fully specified in this extraction.
